subject: Private deployment access-mode synthesis: Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Alice Summers <alice.summers@netgain.com>
To: Evelyn Hart <evelyn.hart@redwood.com>
Cc: NetGain IT <netgain-it@netgain.com>
Date: 2026-11-28T09:12:00-08:00
Subject: Quick ask — recommended connection mode for Private deployment

Hi Evelyn,

Thanks again for the demo last week. NetGain's cloud team started mapping requirements for the Private deployment pilot and asked me to get Redwood's recommendation on connectivity. Our primary constraints:
- Data must never traverse the public internet in transit (regulatory).
- We need predictable latency for inference (95th percentile < 40ms).
- Ops team prefers minimal ongoing maintenance overhead.
- We may start in a single AWS account/region but want a path to multi-account/multi-region.

Could you sketch the trade-offs across three options: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site VPN (IPSec)? If you can include a quick note on onboarding effort, monitoring/observability impact, and where we should be conservative vs aggressive, that would be great.

Also attaching our current network diagram.

Appreciate it — Alice
NetGain Logistics
From: Evelyn Hart <evelyn.hart@redwood.com>
To: Alice Summers <alice.summers@netgain.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-11-29T11:03:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Quick ask — recommended connection mode for Private deployment

Alice — thanks for the diagram and the clear constraints. I reviewed with Karthik and Lauren; below is a concise synthesis. I've attached a one-page summary (redwood-access-options-summary.pdf) that you can share with your cloud network folks. High-level picks below — happy to jump on a quick call to walk through.

Summary (quick):
- VPC peering: lowest latency and simplest data path when both sides are in the same cloud provider and region/account topology. Downsides: scaling across many accounts/regions becomes O(N) peering relationships, and cross-account route management adds operational overhead. Not possible to expose a single service endpoint for multiple consumer VPCs without extra proxy/INGRESS. Good when latency budget is tight and topology is relatively static.

- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): preserves service-side control, avoids adding routes into customer RT tables, and provides a single endpoint pattern across accounts. Slightly higher latency than peering (additional ENI/hop) but much simpler for multi-account usage and better isolation. Monitoring at the service endpoint is straightforward; troubleshooting requires ENI-level metrics and flow logs. Recommended when you expect multiple consumer VPCs/accounts or want service-level exposure.

- Site-to-site VPN (IPSec): simplest to get started (existing VPN tech), supports on-prem connectivity easily, but generally has higher and more variable latency and less predictable throughput. Adds NAT/MTU considerations for high-throughput inference. Good as a fallback or for early pilots before provisioning cloud-native constructs.

Onboarding effort & ops:
- Fastest: VPN (hours to a day if NetGain already runs VPN gateways) — good for pilot.
- Middle: PrivateLink (1–2 weeks): requires service endpoint config, NLB/ALB placement, and ENI permissions across accounts.
- Longest: Peering at scale (2+ weeks): simple per-pair setup but operationally heavy to scale and manage cross-account routes.

Observability implications:
- Peering: rely on VPC flow logs + host-level telemetry; tracing requires distributed instrumentation across both sides.
- PrivateLink: can instrument at the service ENI/NLB and collect per-endpoint metrics; cleaner service-level logs.
- VPN: use CloudWatch/VNS if native, but expect less granularity and higher jitter; good to pair with synthetic latency checks.

Failure modes & fallback:
- Recommend an automatic fallback policy at the application layer: prefer peering/privatelink paths; if they fail, route to a hosted fallback in Redwood's hosted region (we can discuss RPO/RTO tradeoffs).

Suggested starting plan for NetGain pilot:
1) Short pilot (2–4 weeks): stand up an IPSec VPN into the Redwood Private control plane for quick validation (low friction).
2) Pilot expansion (weeks 3–6): add a PrivateLink endpoint for the service in your main account so you can measure latency/classify traffic.
3) Production (post-pilot): if single-account and latency is consistently <25ms with peering, consider peering for that account; otherwise standardize on PrivateLink across accounts with automated provisioning.

Next steps: if this direction looks good I can have an internal runbook (step-by-step onboarding) sent over and book a technical walkthrough with our infra engineer (Karthik).

— Evelyn
Head of Solutions — Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Quick ask — recommended connection mode for Private deployment

Adding a few technical bullets from the runtime/infra side:

- Latency profile: For short sequence workloads (<= 128 tokens) every added hop matters. Measured delta: Peering ~ baseline, PrivateLink +6–12ms median, VPN +20–60ms median depending on gateway churn and encryption overhead. If your 95th must be <40ms, PrivateLink can still work if you place the NLB in the same AZ and tune ENI placement; VPN likely only acceptable for non-latency-critical flows.

- Throughput and MTU: VPN introduces fragmentation risk if your packet path includes additional encapsulation. For high QPS inference workloads we recommend testing with realistic load (warm KV cache) and verifying MTU path. If you expect sustained high throughput, favor peering or PrivateLink backed by NLBs with healthy connection draining policies.

- Security posture: PrivateLink reduces exposure surface by avoiding route table changes; it's easier to enforce least privilege (IAM + sec-groups). Peering requires careful route table governance and cross-account IAM controls. VPN requires robust key rotation and monitoring of tunnel health.

- Autoscaling & cold-start: whichever connectivity you pick, ensure your autoscaling decider is co-located with the control plane such that capacity ramping doesn't introduce extra NAT hops. We can provide a template Terraform module to create PrivateLink endpoints and NLB configuration.

Happy to set up a 45-minute tech walkthrough if NetGain wants to validate latency/MTU with an initial test harness.

— Karthik
Senior Solutions Architect — Redwood Inference

Thanks — this is exactly the level we needed. Two quick clarifications from our network team:
1) We plan to start in a single account but will onboard two additional accounts within Q1. Does PrivateLink provisioning automation exist in your infra repo?
2) Is a peering + PrivateLink hybrid ever sensible (peer for high-volume internal accounts, PrivateLink for partner or cross-org access)?

If answers are OK, procurement wants an estimated SOW and timeline to do pilot -> prod. Can you share a draft SOW and an estimate for a 6-week engagement?

Regards,
Alice
From: Evelyn Hart <evelyn.hart@redwood.com>
To: Alice Summers <alice.summers@netgain.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-12-02T14:33:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Quick ask — recommended connection mode for Private deployment

Alice — answers inline and next steps below.

1) PrivateLink automation: yes — we maintain a Terraform module and a small automation shim that provisions the NLB, configures target groups for our Private deployment instances, and creates the interface endpoint service. We’ll share the module link and a short runbook. That module also has a flag to create per-account endpoints from a central account via cross-account IAM principals.

2) Hybrid approach: absolutely — hybrid is common. Typical pattern: peer between core infra accounts where latency matters (internal services), and expose customer-facing inference via PrivateLink to avoid managing many peering relationships and to keep access scoping tight. We can outline a hybrid pattern tailored to your org map.

SOW & timeline: attached a draft SOW (sow-draft-netgain.docx) and a one-page cost/time estimate in the PDF. Short summary: pilot (VPN + perf validation) 1–2 weeks; PrivateLink provisioning + perf tuning 2–3 weeks; production rollout and automation 2–4 weeks depending on number of accounts. Total typical engagement: 5–9 weeks.

If this aligns I’ll schedule a technical kickoff (45–60m) and include our infra engineer (Karthik) and a solutions PM (Lauren) to capture acceptance criteria and gating. Please share a few times next week.

— Evelyn
Head of Solutions — Redwood Inference
